articles.text: In a special meeting tomorrow, January 12, the Piedmont Planning Commission will consider a recommendation to City Council to adopt the 2023-2031 6th Cycle Housing Element, and to adopt the Initial Study-Negative Declaration (IS-ND) for the Element which the City released on December 9, 2022. This is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support this growth. City Council will hold a special meeting on January 30 to consider adopting the Housing Element. The State deadline for cities to adopt a Housing Element or face penalties is January 31. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. articles.text: In late November 2022 New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg wrote, For most of my adult life, antisemites – with exceptions like Pat Buchanan and Mel Gibson – have lacked status in America. The most virulent antisemites tended to hate Jews from below, blaming them for their own failures and disappointments. Now, however, anti-Jewish bigotry, or at least tacit approval of anti-Jewish bigotry, is coming from people with serious power: the leader of a major political party, a famous pop star, and the world’s richest man. Goldberg is not wrong and is not alone in sounding this alarm. Antisemitism is on the rise. Locally, nationally, and globally it threatens the lives of many, and threatens the very well-being of our society. This reality must call the church to action. It is important to recognize that antisemitism is antithetical to both the central message of Christianity and to the meaning of the church’s celebration of the Day of Epiphany on January 6. The central message of Christianity is that God, in Christ, is always and forever demonstrating a boundaryless love for the entire cosmos. Antisemitism collides with this truth. Epiphany celebrates the journey, recorded by the writer of the Gospel of Matthew, of the magi, the astrologers from the east, who, bearing gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh, followed the star to worship the newborn king. The message of Epiphany is that the good news of God’s love is for gentile star-gazers as well as for Jewish families living in an often hostile empire. The message of Epiphany is one of inclusion. The message of the Apostle Paul is essentially an Epiphany message. While he does not reference the journey of the magi, Paul, in many of his writings, emphasizes his belief that there is a place for Jew and Gentile alike in the expansive love of God. He makes it clear that in the eternal love of the Christ, Jew and Gentile are on level ground. articles.text: A fire department truck (left) is stuck in a sinkhole caused by rainstorms at the entrance to Oakland Zoo on December 31. Since January 1, Oakland Zoo has been closed due to a large sinkhole at the entrance to the zoo. Zoo officials estimate they may not be able to complete repairs until January 17. A culvert by the vehicle entrance to the Zoo at Golf Links Road collapsed due to heavy rain and rushing water. The culvert, overburdened by the historic amount of rainfall throughout the region over the new year, serves as a connect for Arroyo Viejo Creek and runs beneath the entry road to the Zoo. The sinkhole is approximately A sinkhole caused by excessive rain and flooding at the entrance to Oakland Zoo. 10 feet wide and approximately 10 feet deep and is impassable to vehicles, prohibiting guests from entering the Zoo. “As a 100-year-old organization, we are reminded that basic infrastructure must continue to be upgraded at the Zoo while disaster preparedness is vital for everyone across the State,” said Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia. “Unfortunately, the Zoo is now losing nearly $500,000 per week in revenue while needing to keep up our expenses to ensure animals and staff are cared for.” Zoo officials are working with a local engineering company to repair the damage. They have been advised that it may take until the third week of the year or longer for materials to arrive and the work to be completed. In other areas of the Zoo on December 31 the volume and velocity of the water flowing across the Zoo grounds caused extensive soil erosion, with eucalyptus trees falling and flooding in some buildings. All animals and staff are fine and have remained safe during the extreme weather. While closed, Zoo staff will continue to be onsite to take care of the animals, provide maintenance needs, and conduct clean-ups from damage caused by the rain. Guests with reservations to visit the Zoo or attend Glowfari will receive an email about a refund or rescheduling their visit. articles.text: Many people are becoming more aware that their daily choices impact the environment and marketers have taken notice. In a survey of people from over 60 countries, Nielsen’s Global Corporate Sustainability Report found that 66% of consumers would spend more on a product if it is marketed as sustainable. As a result, companies have a financial incentive to market their products as environmentally friendly – regardless of whether they are taking steps to be more sustainable. What is greenwashing? Greenwashing is a marketing tactic that involves using unsubstantiated claims to present a product as eco-friendly. Greenwashing undermines companies that are engaged in sustainable business practices and, by extension, the consumer’s ability to vote with their dollar. Look further into a company’s claims If you see a claim that you’re dubious about, go to the company’s website to investigate further. If you can’t find any record of it or if the information is vague, it’s likely an example of greenwashing. Watch out for terms with no clear meaning These include terms such as “eco-friendly,” “green,” “all-natural,” “earth-friendly,” “nontoxic,” “plant-based,” “plant-derived,” “pure,” “raw,” “healthy,” “biodegradable,” and “organic” (without certification). These words don’t have any legal or technical definition, and therefore don’t say anything concrete about whether a product is truly environmentally friendly. Look for well-known certifications Certifications such as “Fair Trade Cer tif ied,” “USDA Organic,” “Non-GMO Project Verified,” “Rainforest Alliance Certified,” and “Certified B Corporation” are all trustworthy labels. Don’t fall for the “lesser of two evils” concept For example, a fashion label creating a sustainable collection is better than the brand ignoring the subject of sustainability entirely, but it doesn’t change the fact that the fast-fashion business model is inherently unsustainable. Beware of irrelevant claims An example of an irrelevant claim is a company that claims their product is “CFC Free”. Since chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are banned by law, they wouldn’t be found in the product regardless. The marketing tactic is to imply a choice that does not exist. Buy fewer things According to data from the University of California, Berkeley and its consumption emission analysis firm EcoDataLab, Piedmonters have among the highest consumption emission rates in the country. Even if the products you’re buying are more eco-friendly than alternatives, the best thing for the environment is to buy less. Look further into a company’s claims If you see a claim that you’re dubious about, go to the company’s website to investigate further. If you can’t find any record of it or if the information is vague, it’s likely an example of greenwashing. Watch out for terms with no clear meaning These include terms such as “eco-friendly,” “green,” “all-natural,” “earth-friendly,” “nontoxic,” “plant-based,” “plant-derived,” “pure,” “raw,” “healthy,” “biodegradable,” and “organic” (without certification). These words don’t have any legal or technical definition, and therefore don’t say anything concrete about whether a product is truly environmentally friendly. Look for well-known certifications Certifications such as “Fair Trade Cer tif ied,” “USDA Organic,” “Non-GMO Project Verified,” “Rainforest Alliance Certified,” and “Certified B Corporation” are all trustworthy labels. Don’t fall for the “lesser of two evils” concept For example, a fashion label creating a sustainable collection is better than the brand ignoring the subject of sustainability entirely, but it doesn’t change the fact that the fast-fashion business model is inherently unsustainable. Beware of irrelevant claims An example of an irrelevant claim is a company that claims their product is “CFC Free”. Since chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are banned by law, they wouldn’t be found in the product regardless. The marketing tactic is to imply a choice that does not exist. Buy fewer things According to data from the University of California, Berkeley and its consumption emission analysis firm EcoDataLab, Piedmonters have among the highest consumption emission rates in the country. Even if the products you’re buying are more eco-friendly than alternatives, the best thing for the environment is to buy less. articles.text: Staff photos Staff photos Nicholas Christ recently was hired as a new member of the Piedmont Fire Department. Nicholas “Niko” Christ and Nadder Shehadeh have joined the Piedmont Fire Department as firefighter-paramedics. Nicholas Christ Christ began his career in mid- 2016 as an EMT in Napa County, where he was raised. After three years he moved to Santa Rosa and worked as an EMT for a private ambulance service. Wanting to expand his career to include firefighting, he moved to Winters, west of Sacramento, and attended its fire academy. After graduating in February, he began working in Piedmont. “I’ve never been part of a city that regards their public services and public servants so well,” said Christ. “I feel spoiled by the way the community here treats us, and I really take pride in giving back to that community.” Christ knew that he wanted to be a firefighter as soon as he began EMT school in Napa seven years ago. “I wanted to make sure I was a good paramedic before I took on any more responsibility. After all, more than 70% of the calls we take here are medical.” Much of Christ’s family still lives in Napa, and he still resides with his girlfriend in Winters. Nevertheless, he has every intenNadder Shehadeh is a new firefighter-paramedic with the Piedmont Fire Department. tion of continuing to work in Piedmont over the years to come. “This is my first full experience as a firefighter, and there’s been such a change and increase of responsibility on the job compared to my experience of training for it,” he said. “Regardless, Piedmont has been a great place to start this new part of my career. I really feel accepted by everyone here.” Nadder Shehadeh Although Shehadeh was born in northern California, he was raised in Palestine. In 2006, when he was 10, his parents moved back to California to an eightacre property in Placer County that they had purchased in the 1980s. With his father and four brothers, Shehadeh built stables and arenas and began a horse ranch business which continues to this day under the name Boarding on the Lake. The ranch, located in Granite Bay, borders Folsom Lake and currently has over 50 horses. After high school, Shehadeh earned his EMT certification. In 2019, he attended the fire academy at Sierra College in Rocklin. He worked for one year with the South Placer Fire District; and after that, three seasons with Cal Fire. “While that work wasn’t particularly stressful, there was a lot on my plate for those years,” said Shehadeh. “Honestly, I initially stuck with it because I’d been working at the horse ranch since I was 10, and I wanted something different.” Nevertheless, Shehadeh is “still definitely very hands-on at the ranch.” He still helps with everyday tasks. This week he will be helping his brothers repair fences and clear fallen trees in the wake of damage caused by the recent rainstorms. “Where I grew up in Placer County,” Shehadeh said, “Folsom, Roseville, and Granite Bay were similar to Piedmont in that they were all small, tight-knit communities.” He concurs with Christ that “the community is a lot more family-oriented here, compared to other departments nearby, like Oakland. I’m very lucky to have started this job in Piedmont, and I’d like to see out my career here.” HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Piedmont students ranked first amongst all K-12 California public school districts in Science, with 75% “meeting or exceeding” the state standards on the 2022 California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) standardized test. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language Arts/Literacy, Mathematics and now, Science. The CAASPP replaced the paperbased Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. In addition, PUSD’s percentage of 5th- and 8th-graders who “met or exceeded” state standards was the highest in the state of all K-12 and K-8 school districts. In comparison, 40% of students in Alameda County and 29.45% of students in California met or exceeded state science standards. Piedmont students also ranked among the top three K-12 school districts in California in English Language Arts and Math. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and 11, participated in the 2021-22 CAASPP for English Language Arts and Math, while students in grades 5, 8, and 12, participated in the California Science Test (CAST). The school district showed an improvement of more than six percentage points from the previous year and is higher than its pre-pandemic performance in 2018-19. Met or Exceeded’ Science Percentages: 2018-19 70.11% 2019-20 No Data due to COVID 2020-21 68.86% 2021-22 74.95% To view full results, visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcast2022. “We congratulate our students for their outstanding performance on the California Science Test and setting the standard among school districts in the state,” said PUSD Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “In addition, much appreciation to our educators for their dedication in finding innovative methods to teach this important subject and help our students succeed.” Like class assignments and report cards, the CAASPP assessments are one gauge of measuring student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. Individual student score reports were made available in the fall and can be accessed at anytime by families on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. articles.text: James Clear, author of Atomic Habits, in one of my absolute favorite quotes about goals says, “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” As we enter the season of new year’s resolutions, which are basically goals in bunny ear disguises, I often think of Clear’s concise description of why resolutions don’t work. We can resolve all we want, but if we don’t create the systems to scaffold those resolutions, there is no way that those resolutions will get past January 17th. If your goals are around exercise and eating healthy, there are millions of “systems” that appear this time of year: “30 days to a Healthy You,” advertises your gym, “Yoga Fit in 45 Days,” screams a new app, “Clean Eating One Day at a Time.” a new diet program calls out. But what happens if your goals are less concrete? What if you desire a life that has more creativity? A worldview that is less binary and more open? What if joy and connection with others is the resolution? Daily creative expression can help move us towards all of those things, but using Clear’s guidance, it requires systems, not just goals. Here are some ideas for how to give structure and scaffolding to your creative goals: • Choose something small that you can add into your daily routine and tag it on to something you are already doing. For instance, if you already spend five minutes reviewing and updating your to-do list every morning, add 10 minutes to start a color journal where you just explore one color each day with watercolor. • Find something that you enjoy, like a dance class or zumba and mark it on your calendar weekly. Make it sacred. The same way that you would never schedule over Thanksgiving dinner, this weekly appointment cannot be moved. Make sure everyone at work and in your family understands that this is a non-negotiable. • Calendar in creative breaks, the same way you might give yourself a 5 minute stretch break in between zooms, change half of those stretch times to creative times. Put on a song you enjoy listening to and sing along, doodle a fun little cartoon for your kids, dance between your desk and the bathroom…whatever feels fun and easy. I hope your new year’s resolutions turn into systems and structures that last a lifetime. And, if they don’t…you can always declare a new month’s resolution, a new week’s resolution or even a new day’s resolution. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Coach and Speaker. You can view her latest Tedx Talk at https://youtu.be/ ITM2oD2mhR0. New Year’s resolutions require systems, not just goals.

articles.text: At a moving reception and concert dedication filled with song, words, and love for the recipient, longtime board member Sue Malick was presented with the Founder’s Award by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir at its Candlelight Concert on December 10 at First Congregational Church in Berkeley. The award was created to honor and acknowledge individuals who have shown exceptional commitment and extraordinary service in the choral community. Past recipients include founder Suzie Rahl, founding artistic Directors Bob Geary and Sue Bohlin, as well as standout volunteers including Paul & Andrea Swenson, Ray Perman, Terry Amgott-Kwan, and the Munich family. “At the heart of our work are the connections and the loving community we create through music, as many voices sound as one. Sue Malick’s warmth, advocacy, and dedication to the Choirs on behalf of children and youth from Richmond to Oakland to Piedmont and beyond exemplify our values. Whether championing homestays for entire tours, opening her heart and home to staff and board, for decades she has authentically and earnestly cared for everyone within our community. Honoring her with this award is a delight and rare privilege,” said current Executive Director Keri Butkevich. A reception was held across the street at First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley prior to the evening concert. Many well wishes sent prior to the event reflected on Sue’s contributions to both Choir and community, including the Malick family hosting large groups of Piedmont Sue Malick was presented with the Founder’s Award honored in December for her long support of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. choristers at their home in Hochhausen, Germany since 2018. “Sue is an amazing contributor to so much of our local culture. She is smart, energetic, and very talented”,” said Carol Brown. During the concert and reception, Malick was gifted a quilt of homes, honoring her commitment to securing homestays for the triennial international Golden Gate Festival hosted in the East Bay for many years. She was also presented with an engraved stein connecting to her deep roots in Hochhausen and the local community. Prior to the Choirs and community singing the traditional Estonian song “Ta Elagu” (Long Life), Artistic Director Eric Tuan thanked Malick for her decades-long devotion to PEBCC. “Over the past four decades, Sue has dedicated herself to building the Choir community through her generous hospitality, inclusive welcome, and gracious spirit. She has been one of the longest-serving members of the Board of Directors; she has hosted countless receptions for members of the Choir community and for our visiting guests from abroad; and she has volunteered whenever and wherever her help was needed,” said Tuan. “Thank you for all you have done for our community over the past four decades,” he added. In her time on the board, Malick has seen the organization grow from a local Piedmont group in its earliest years, to an internationally acclaimed K-12 youth Choral music organization serving close to 300 singers from 90 schools and 23 Bay Area communities. To learn more about how your family can become part of the Choirs, visit www.piedmontchoirs.org/.

Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: Coach Ben Spencer’s talented basketball team returned from winter break and immediately posted a satisfactory 62-46 win against St. Joseph in Alameda on Friday, January 6. It marked the team’s first game against a Western Alameda County Conference opponent and improved its record to 9-3. It was a close game through the first one-and-a-half quarters with the game deadlocked 18-18 in the second quarter. But Piedmont began taking over the game to lead 30-23 by halftime, including a strong defensive fourth quarter to allow just four points. “What is great about our program is that every team is going to give us their best. I think people circle Piedmont on their calendars now, which wasn’t always the case. Tonight, I thought we were really good defensively. St. Joe made a lot of tough shots and we nearly held them under 40 points – that’s a goal of ours (this season) to hold teams under 40,” said Spencer. Good ball movement resulted in finding Brit Burden at the top of the key and A.J. Harris working his way around the court. Harris finished with 30 points and Burden had 19. “We knew this was going to be a battle, St. Joseph is such a renowned program. We knew not to get worried if it was a close game early and to just continue to play our brand of basketball,” said Harris. “They were having two guys extend out and left the middle open, so Brit would get the ball in the middle and drew a lot of contact.” “I think their zone defense rattled us at the beginning, but we just stayed with the game plan. Shots started to fall, we started working well with each other. They ran a 2-3 zone but the middle guy wasn’t staying close to me at the free throw line, so we were able to run our offense through the middle,” said Burden. Game Recap The two sides were tied at 14-14 to end the first quarter, but Piedmont jumped ahead 30-23 by halftime. St. Joseph narrowed the gap to 45-41 to start the fourth quarter, but PHS dominated defensively in the final going, allowing the Pilots just four points while the Highlanders scored 17. With the game tied 18-18 through the early portion of the second quarter, Piedmont went on a 9-2 scoring run to go ahead 27-20. The Pilots added a 3-pointer to make it 27-23, but Harris tacked on three more points via free throws, 30-23. In the third quarter, St. Joes came out hot to score seven of the next nine points to put themselves within one possession at 32-30, but that is at close as things would get. From there, Piedmont put up eight of the next nine of the next 12 points to lead 41-33. However, the quarter ended with PHS holding a narrow 45-41 lead. A.J. Harris finished with 30 points against St. Joseph. Staff Photos Brit Burden scored 19 points in Piedmont’s return.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team finished 2022 in style by winning the SoCal Holiday Prep Classic’s premier division December 27-30 at San Diego’s Canyon Hills HS. They won four games, including 60-42 over ‘Iolani of Hawaii, 82-69 over Rancho Christian of Temecula, had a narrow 55-54 win over Westview of San Diego in the semifinals, and won their division with a 83-67 victory over Centennial of Corona. Piedmont’s Natalia Martinez and Eva Levingston named to the All-Tournament team. Piedmont is off to one of its strongest seasons since winning the State championship with the Paris twins in 2004 and 2005, The team currently is undefeated at 11-0. “This is a great team,” exuded coach Bryan Gardere, “We have a lot of eyes on us and strong teams always get a lot of invitations to high-level tournaments. It’s been a great start to the season and now we go into our league schedule.” PHS beats Centennial 83-67 for tourney title Piedmont jumped out to a 21-11 lead after the first quarter and 41-31 by halftime. They extended the gap to 60-48 in the third quarter and closed out the game with 23 points in the fourth quarter, conceding just 19 to finish 83-67. All of Piedmont’s eight players finished with points. Final scorers include: Trinity Zamora led the way with 28 points, Martinez finished with 22, Levingston had 18, Maddie Hill scored five, Shakila Zuberi and Adrienne Blackwell had three, Perseas Gioukaris had four, and Samantha Smith had two. One-point barnburner vs. Westview In a razor-thin close semifinal, Piedmont trailed 16-13 at the end of the first quarter but went ahead 34-33 by halftime. The Highlanders struggled in the third quarter and were outscored 17-6 to allow Westview a 10-point advantage, 50-40. But with a strong rally in the last quarter, Piedmont’s defense limited Westview to four points, wnd its offense did the job with 15 points. Zamora led with 13 points, Martinez had 12, Levingston had nine, Gioukaris and Hill had eight points, while Blackwell scored five. 82-69 over Rancho Christian Piedmont trailed 19-15 to end the first quarter but stormed ahead for a 38-34 lead at the half. PHS then exploded for 29 points in the third quarter to put the game away. They entered the fourth quarter leading 67-49 and added 15 points to close out the victory. Staff Photo Trinity Zamora scored 28 points in the championship game with Centennial. Eva Levingston (left) and Natalia Martinez were named to the AllTournament team in San Diego. Final scorers include: Martinez had 22 points, Levingston scored 16, Hill had 13, Zamora had 15, Zuberi had eight, and Gioukaris had seven. 60-42 over ‘Iolani Piedmont built a 22-10 lead in the first quarter and made it 36-23 by halftime. PHS only scored 10 in the third but held Iolani to seven points to make it 46-30 to start the fourth. They added 14 points in the final going for the 60-42 win. Final scorers include: Levingston had 17 points, Martinez scored 15, Zamora had nine, Blackwell scored seven, Hill and Zuberi each had six. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley Piedmont started the league portion of its schedule last night, Tuesday, January 10, against Castro Valley. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (11-0) heads to Alameda tomorrow, Thursday, January 12 for a 6:30 p.m. game. In a historic first, they will play in MLK Showcases at two locations, facing San Joaquin Memorial at St. Mary’s of Stockton on Saturday, January 14 at 9:00 p.m. and Salesian at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Monday, January 16 at 2:00 p.m.

articles.text: Junior striker Aiden Woolwine calls out directions. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team lost a 2-0 decision to North Coast Section foe Cardinal Newman in Santa Rosa on Friday, January 6. It was the first time Piedmont faced Cardinal Newman since the season-opener last season, a scoreless draw. “The score line might not reflect that it was a close game. I think we deserved a result. We’re hoping to get them again in NCS,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. In the early minutes the Cardinals scored on a set piece, and was similar to their game-winning goal in the second round of the NCS playoffs in 2020. From there, Piedmont pressed forward for the goal but were unable to find the finishing touch—including one attempt that rang hard off of the crossbar. “We played it tight after that point. articles.text: Margo Donahue (left), PHS Class of 2019, has earned a spot on the United States’ Under-24 Ultimate Frisbee team. In the growing sport of Ultimate Frisbee, there is no greater honor than representing your country. Competing in the 2023 World Flying Disc Federation from July 1-8 in England will be Piedmont native and current U.C. Davis senior Margo Donahue as a member of the U.S. Women’s Under-24 team. The tournament is essentially the World Cup of Ultimate Frisbee. “The U-24 level tends to be the best college players competing in the whole world. The United States historically does really well because we’re the leading country in the Ultimate Frisbee world. For U-24, the United States has won 11 out of 12 opportunities in all divisions of men’s, women’s, and mixed Ultimate. The U.S. team is always the team to beat,” said Donahue. She plays on multiple teams, including U.C. Davis’ women’s club team, a mixed team called the San Francisco Polar Bears, and another mixed club team in Davis called the Davis Heatwave. Of those, the Polar Bears are a nationally ranked team. Getting noticed from the United States required her to attend a tryout in November in San Diego where she impressed the coaches enough to get a spot. “After you apply and get accepted, there is a West coast and East coast tryout, and then it’s a matter of being selected by the coaches. There’s a pool of around 200 people who tryout and maybe around 1,000 who apply. Donahue, 1 2018 graduated of Piedmont High, has been competing in the sport competitively for the past seven years but feels like she was destined to play since before her birth given her parents met playing while playing. “I’ve been playing seven years competitively, but my parents actually met playing Ultimate, so it’s been in my life a long time. I played on a youth club team during high school and then once I got to college, I started on the women’s team. The rest is hisMargo Donahue (left) will compete in the 2023 World Flying Disc Federation in England, the sport’s equivalent of the World Cup. tory. Ultimate has been kind of my whole life after that,” said Donahue. Making the United States team has been a long sought-after accomplishment for Donahue since she picked up a Frisbee to play competitively back in high school. “Competing on the U.S. team on the world stage means a lot to me. It’s something I’ve been dreaming about since I began playing competitively in high school. I would see people on ESPN and think, ‘Wow, these people are just 21 years old and getting Gold.’ It’s something I’ve been thinking about since I was 15 and now that I’m on the team, it’s kind of insane to me,” said Donahue. Ultimate Frisbee, known simply as Ultimate, is a fast-growing sport all over the world. As Donahue describes, the culture of the sport is nothing like anything she’s experienced after being a varsity runner at Piedmont High’s track and cross country teams. “Ultimate is special in that it’s such a positive and supportive community. One of the biggest aspects that drew me to Ultimate is something we call, ‘The Spirit of the Game.’ When you play the game, you compete with respect, integrity, and honesty. Ultimate Frisbee began as a self-refereed sport and in many cases still is. Our referees are called Observers, who don’t usually make call but are just there to clarify rules. A lot is on the players to make calls themselves with integrity and honesty. Everyone treats everyone with respect. The idea behind Ultimate is we’re playing the most competitively we can be while being the most respectful people we can, that culture is really held up around the world,” said Donahue. Margo Donahue leaps to grab the Frisbee. She is a senior at U.C. Davis and previously ran track and cross country at Piedmont High.

articles.text: Dunkirk is a stretching expanse of sandy beach on the northernmost tip of France. There is a shallow-water harbor with a long breakwater pier called “the mole.” If you look toward the horizon, just 28 miles across the Strait of Dover, you can almost see England and its iconic white Between May 26 and June 4, 1940, before the Battle for Britain, before America entered the war, some 400,000 allied troops – Brits, Canadians, French and Belgians – were gathered on that immense Dunkirk beach, waiting. Most stood in long, ragged lines, others sat at the water’s edge, in the foamy white water. Countless soldiers crowded shoulder to shoulder on the mole, desperately hoping to be ferried out to ships that had yet to arrive. Behind them, advancing ever closer, was the full might of the German army which had already invaded Poland, Denmark, Norway, Belgium and now France. Its objective was to capture or annihilate these men now in full And in the grey-blue sky above, often obscured by a hazy sun, were the German Luftwaffe, remorselessly bombing and strafing the exposed soldiers. This moment in British history is now the stuff of myth. While it was, indisputably a retreat, a A scene from Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk. graphic statement of defeat, it was also viewed in its totality as heroic, a prelude to events that will never be forgotten. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan, Dunkirk is shot in large format film (not digital), it conveys the feel and the texture of the men, as well as the urgency of their dilemma. The terrifying problem for them, for the officers standing on the mole, for those in England (to include Churchill) was: is rescue possible? To simply leave them there was unimaginable and would likely change the course of the war. Nolan approaches his narrative from three points of view: the beach, the sea, and the air. On the beach are the soldiers, their isolation total; in the air are the British Spitfires, especially two whose mission it was to provide defense against the German bombers and Messerschmidts; and on the sea were the ships. What is remarkable is that a call went out by the English command for help, of any kind. An ad hoc flotilla was quickly assembled – tugs, trawlers, merchant ships, fishing boats, weekender yachts, small motor boats – all leaving England without hesitation, headed for Dunkirk and the stranded troops. Their mission was to ferry the troops to those few waiting ships. Other small craft would return to England directly, laden with desperate, oil- soaked, traumatized soldiers. Of course, we as Americans know the story of D-Day. Many have seen Steven Spielberg’s astonishingly good Saving Private Ryan. And what we know is that the allied troops that landed on those harrowing beaches of France, on that early June, 1944, day, were advancing, headed onto shore and beyond. It was an army of liberation, prepared to fight a long, deadly battle against fascism. There was dread, every day of the war, shrouded by a carnage that we cannot imagine. But the direction was clear. Dunkirk involved a different quality of dread, which the film graphically conveys with its minimalist dialogue, its ensemble of actors that are all but indistinguishable, with the exception of naval Commander Bolton, portrayed by Kenneth Branagh, or the two Spitfire pilots who gaze down on the beaches and know that their mission possesses an overwhelming urgency. What is remarkable about Nolan’s film is that while we are witnessing a stark retreat, we are also bearing witness to astonishing heroism; the two never feel contradictory. Dunkirk is beautifully photographed by cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema, its narrative balanced between one hour in the air, one day on the sea and one week on that excruciatingly memorable beach at Dunkirk. According to its creators, Matt and Ross Duffer, this series was, from the outset, influenced by the works of Steven Spielberg, Stephen King, Wes Craven, and H.P. Lovecraft and has attracted a record-setting Netflix viewership/fanbase. It’s earned high praise for its creepy, chilling atmosphere, superb acting, excellent directing and exceptional writing. It has also received a bevy of awards and nominations, to include the Golden Globes, the Directors Guild of America Awards, The British Academy Television Awards, and the People’s Choice Awards. Stranger Things is set in a small mid-western town called Hawkins. The time is the 1980s, and the narrative opens with quasi-supernatural forces, all of which are connected to the nondescript Hawkins National Laboratory. The lab is known to carry out not just government research, but is rumored to conduct under the radar experiments into the paranormal using human subjects. The lab inadvertently creates a portal to another dimension referred to as the “Upside Down” that has an unanticipated effect on the residents of Hawkins in calamitous ways. Season 1, episode one, begins with the abduction of tween Will Byer (Noah Schnapp) by a creature from the Upside Down. And it’s his mother, Joyce (Winona Ryder), and the Chief of Police Hopper (David Harbour) who set out to find him. And thus begins what proves to be a remarkable adventure that has captured audiences’ imaginations, season after season. Stranger Things. Written and produced by Matt and Ross Duffer, aka the Duffer Bros. articles.text: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2, released in 2011, is the eighth and last film in a series that began the same year that the twin towers fell in New York. It’s been a remarkable ride, these movies and books, in the aggregate a stunning achievement, unequaled in sheer breadth and depth. It was J.K. Rowling who wrote seven volumes totaling some 4200 pages, each book resonating with her fans, all those young Potterheads. From the depths of her imagination, she created a cultural phenomenon that remains thus far unrivaled. Youngsters sat outside of bookstores at midnight, wearing peepers and pointed hats, carrying wands, waiting for the next book, often a tome the size of the New York phone book. Each was quickly devoured and discussed. The eight films, waited for with delicious anticipation, comprise 20 hours of screen time and have generated some $7 billion in box office receipts. All of this begs the question: Why? What is there about an orphaned boy, Harry Potter, sent off to wizard school by his disgruntled Muggle relatives, to a place named, improbably, Hogwarts? Perhaps it’s as simple as Harry possessing a magical power and an abiding fearlessness, something that every young person would delight in having. As the series progresses, as multiple narrative strands are gradually brought together, Harry prepares to confront his nemesis, Lord Voldermot. And so we arrive at part two of the final film. For all those Potterheads who have passed the last fourteen years immersed in the labyrinthine adventures of Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) and Hermione (Emma Watson) and Ron (Rupert Grint), this last film will be bittersweet. The long, rambling narrative could easily have been brought to the screen as a series of B-movies. Instead, each film has been lavishly crafted and richly produced and adapted. Part two of Deathly Hallows may be the best of the eight. It is intense and astonishingly good. As are the English actors who have, at the insistence of Rowling, peopled the franchise from the outset. Of course, when walking in to the theater, it helps to have been immersed in Potter lore. Which is no small thing. You need more than a program to get current; you need a wizard dictionary. For some filmgoers, part two will merely amaze. As for the already initiated, and even the recently ordained, this last installment will be captivating. It dazzles as the climax draws near and as Harry moves ever closer to that moment when he may, indeed, die at the hands (or wand) of He Who Shall Not Be Named. Of course, the outcome is known to those who have read the seventh book; but no matter. It is all wonderful and again wonderful and an appropriately soaring finale. As an aside: In a scene from act three, Dumbledore says to Harry, “Words are our most inexhaustible source of magic.” Indeed. Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2. Directed by David Yates. Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint. 2 hrs., 11 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now sStreaming on VUDU/Prime/ peacock/ HBO max.

No profession cherishes its child prodigies more than does the world of classical music. You never hear of child prodigies in rock and roll, nor are there any in country and western music. Nope. But classical music has had Mozarts and Mendelssohns, and a host of others. San Francisco is notable for having given the musical world four of the greatest violinists of all time. The first was Yehudi Menuhin. Then in close succession came Ruggiero Ricci and Grisha Goluboff. Isaac Stern followed soon after. articles.text: A contrafact is a new melody written on an existing chord progression. The tradition is based on contrafactum (from Medieval Latin contrafacere, to counterfeit). Religious vocal works in Europe were modified by changing the lyric text from sacred to secular. For example, What Child Is This was changed to Greensleeves. Contrafacta was used in hymns in fourth-century Syria, seventh-eleventh century Palestine and Constantinople, tenth century Byzantium, and in twelfth and thirteenth century West European secular song (troubadours, trouvères and Minnesinger). A parody mass, from the 16th century, uses multiple voices of pre-existing piece of music, such as a fragment of a motet or a secular chanson. The U.S. Copyright Law of 1909 protects a composer’s rights to lyrics and melody, but not chord progression, unless the chord progression is very unique. The 1909 law said that the publication of a sound recording did not publish the musical work. To get rights to the song, you had to submit a notated copy of the music. In the decades that followed, record companies would hire people to make those manuscripts, allowing them to pay the musicians per recording and claim all rights to the songs themselves. Louis Armstrong said: “They used to either buy the tune outright, or ask us if we cared to collect the royalties… Of course you don’t have to make any guesses as to our decisions… Aye?… Sure… Our slogan was ‘A bird in hand gathers no moss.’” Publishing houses would sometimes purchase songs from songwriters in exchange for exposure of their songs to producers, musical directors, and commercial radio networks. In the 1940s, beboppers came up with a solution to the problem of having to pay the composers and to be able to get their own royalties: they wrote new melodies on chord progressions of standards, which we call “contrafacts.” Here’s a list of jazz contrafacts: https://en.wikipedia.org/ wiki/List_of_ jazz_contrafacts. I was his concert master for many years, and was always impressed by Edgar the man, and Edgar the musician. He was without a doubt, the most generous and open-minded musician I have ever known. He was sincere, and always kept his word. I was also impressed by his musicianship. Under Braun’s leadership, the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra was immensely successful. The concerts were always well attended, and the quality of the music making was always very high. Upon Edgar Braun’s retirement and death, leadership passed to Ben Simon. The January 1 concert at St. Marks Episcopal Church in Palo Alto was a mixed affair. A large audience overflowed the church. Musically speaking, the concert was very professional. As a conductor, Simon loves to talk. articles.text: A hardy group of 14 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays got lucky last Wednesday and beat the incoming rain by several hours. Nancy and Mike Henn led the walk for Dick Carter who had missed several weeks due to a medical procedure. The plan was to stay in central Piedmont, but if there was no serious rain the route could be extended – exactly what happened. The group went up Highland Avenue to Guilford Road and onto Requa Road and Hazel Lane. It was recalled this was once the entrance to a historical spot. At the start of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have good educations, so she got Isaac Requa to build a one-room schoolhouse on his property at what is now the Requa Place cul-de-sac. Amy Long hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children for the first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Amy leased a house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and California families and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913. However, the Stock Market crashed in 1929 and the Depression created financial difficulties for many parents. Piedmont High, which opened in 1921, was less expensive and the Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and it closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The group walked to the tall redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, where the entrance to the Ransom Bridges School once was. The walkers went through the Hazel Lane loop to the school’s former site at 141 Hazel Lane. Walker Jim Kellogg, an architect, expressed admiration for the Albert Farr craftsman design of the home, including the beauty of the stone wall in front and the house’s copper gutters. The walkers continued to Piedmont Court, walking on the sidewalk behind the wide strip of grass that was once a Key System train track. At Piedmont Court they noted a birdhouse in a front yard that is a miniature of the actual house. A path at the end of the Piedmont Court cul-de-sac took the walkers to Mountain Avenue. The rain had not yet begun so the group went to Piedmont Park to see how much water was flowing in Bushy Dell Creek. There was a good flow, but the group knew more was going to come soon. Taking the park path behind Piedmont High School, they went through the high school campus, past the library and student center where they could see San Francisco and the clouds and rain on their way. The walkers had a dry, almost two-mile leisurely walk in about an hour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers showed up at the Exedra on Wednesday, January 4, prepared for a stroll in the rain. The walkers included Jim Kuo, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Jane Holland with K-9 best friend Sasha, Rob Smith, Karen Palmer, Melba Yee, Alicia Rivera, Priscilla Wanerus, Albert Chen, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, and Nancy and Mike Henn with their K-9 best friend Roger. A resident of the city for more than 50 years, he was a loving husband and the father of two daughters. Born on March 29, 1941 in Santa Monica, California, he was the son of Elsie June and Vance Wolfe. He grew up in Redwood City where he attended Sequoia High School. In 1957 Bruce and his wife-to-be, Linda, met at First Christian Church camp in Redwood City and began their life-long love. They married on September 2, 1962 and gave birth to their first daughter, Heather in 1966. They moved to Piedmont, in 1967 and welcomed their second child, Hilary, in 1968. Bruce studied art at San Jose State University and the Art Institute of San Francisco. Additionally, he studied with renowned artists Bettina Steinke and Bruno Lucchesi. Adept in both oils and Piedmont artist and sculptor Bruce Wolfe. clay, he taught figure painting and sculpture at several Northern California art schools. Bruce was a fellow in the National Sculpture Society and received an honorary doctorate from the Academy of Art in San Francisco. That effort caught the eye of Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. Over the years, Phil has developed relationships with major cartoonists familiar with The New Yorker readers, such as Roz Chast. Last year Phil met Garry Trudeau, creator of “Doonesbury,” and reminded him that Garry was one of the judges in a cartoon contest that named Phil as one of the winners when he was just starting out as a cartoonist. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. “Even most of the ‘regular’ cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time,” Phil noted. Phil was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. “I’ve met very talented people at the annual meetings, including people working in TV animation like ‘The Simpsons,’ graphic novelists, and editorial cartoonists.” Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. Phil has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. “There’s even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of my cartoons in their permanent collection,” he added with a laugh. Phil also volunteers as a presenter for Career Day at elementary and middle schools in Oakland.
